sections.title: Mission · Command Line Basics
paragraphs: Learn how to interact with Linux through the command line, how commands are structured, how Bash handles variables, and how quoting changes text interpretation.
sections.callout: USER → SHELL → LINUX

sections.title: What Is a Shell?
paragraphs: A shell is a command interpreter. It interprets what a user enters and tells the operating system what should happen. Linux supports multiple shells; one of the most important is Bash.
sections.callout: SHELL = COMMAND INTERPRETER

sections.title: Bash
paragraphs: Bash stands for Bourne Again Shell. It is a widely used Linux shell that can run commands, work with files, use variables, execute scripts, recall command history, and chain commands and utilities.
sections.callout: Common Linux command interpreter → Bash

sections.title: Command-Line Syntax
paragraphs: Linux commands commonly follow command option argument. In ls -l /home, ls is the command, -l is the option, and /home is the argument. Not every command requires all three.
sections.callout: COMMAND = WHAT · OPTION = HOW · ARGUMENT = TARGET

entries.title: Commands
paragraphs: The command names the program or operation to execute, such as echo, ls, cd, cp, or rm. Linux generally expects precise syntax.

entries.title: Options
paragraphs: Options modify command behavior and commonly begin with - or --. Do not assume the same option means the same thing for every command.

entries.title: Arguments
paragraphs: Arguments give the command something to work with, such as Hello in echo Hello or /home in cd /home.

sections.title: The echo Command
paragraphs: echo displays text or variable values. For example, echo Hello outputs Hello. It is useful for observing how the shell processes text.
sections.callout: ECHO = DISPLAY TEXT OR A VALUE

sections.title: Variables
paragraphs: A variable stores a value for later reference. After name=GSA, echo $name outputs GSA. The $ tells the shell to retrieve the stored value.
sections.callout: VARIABLE = LABELED BOX · $VARIABLE = OPEN THE BOX

sections.title: Exam Trap — Variable Assignment Syntax
paragraphs: Shell variable assignment is syntax-sensitive. name=GSA is not equivalent to casually inserting spaces around the equals sign.
sections.callout: SHELL SYNTAX MATTERS

sections.title: Environment Variables
paragraphs: An environment variable stores information used by the shell and programs. PATH is an especially important example.
sections.callout: ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES INFORM THE SHELL AND PROGRAMS

sections.title: PATH
paragraphs: PATH tells the shell which directories to search for executable commands. When you type ls without its complete executable path, the shell searches directories listed in PATH. Inspect it with echo $PATH.
sections.callout: Directories searched for executable programs → PATH

sections.title: Why PATH Matters
paragraphs: If a program is stored in a directory not included in PATH, entering only the program name may not locate it. You may need its full path, a PATH change, or correct installation and configuration.
sections.callout: COMMAND EXISTS DOES NOT MEAN THE SHELL KNOWS WHERE IT IS

sections.title: export
paragraphs: export makes a shell variable available to programs and subshells launched from that environment. For example: export NAME=GSA.
sections.callout: EXPORT = MAKE A VARIABLE AVAILABLE TO CHILD PROCESSES

sections.title: Quoting
paragraphs: Quoting controls how the shell interprets text, including special characters such as $, spaces, and wildcards. The two important styles are double quotes and single quotes.
sections.callout: QUOTING CONTROLS INTERPRETATION

sections.title: Double Quotes
paragraphs: Double quotes preserve text as one argument while still allowing expansions such as variables. If name=GSA, echo "Welcome $name" can output Welcome GSA.
sections.callout: DOUBLE QUOTES = VARIABLES CAN STILL SPEAK

sections.title: Single Quotes
paragraphs: Single quotes treat enclosed text more literally. If name=GSA, echo 'Welcome $name' can display Welcome $name rather than replacing the variable.
sections.callout: SINGLE QUOTES = KEEP IT LITERAL

sections.title: Exam Trap — Single vs. Double Quotes
sections.callout: DOUBLE = EXPAND · SINGLE = LITERAL

sections.title: Spaces and Quoting
paragraphs: Quoting groups text containing spaces into one argument. echo "Giant Slayer Academy" treats the quoted phrase together. This is especially important for filenames containing spaces.
sections.callout: QUOTES KEEP SPACED TEXT TOGETHER

sections.title: history
paragraphs: history displays previously executed shell commands. It helps repeat commands, troubleshoot, remember syntax, and review earlier work.
sections.callout: Display previously entered commands → history

sections.title: type
paragraphs: type identifies how the shell interprets a command name, such as a shell builtin, alias, or external executable. type echo helps reveal what Bash will execute.
sections.callout: TYPE = WHAT KIND OF COMMAND IS THIS?

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: Variable available to child processes → export
Determine how Bash interprets a command → type
Variable expansion inside quoted text → Double quotes
Literal text without variable expansion → Single quotes
sections.callout: Match the command-line need to the shell feature.
